lines.text: Your arm and flywheel can both say whether they've arrived, but nothing waits for that answer yet. A coroutine does. It's a routine that can stop on a line until something comes true.
Four calls build every routine in this course. Two of them start a command, and the other two only wait.
The arm's command never finishes on its own. Await it, and the routine never leaves that line, so anything that runs forever gets forked instead.
Don't drop the little arrow in front of the question. It's what lets the routine ask again on every loop, instead of asking once and keeping a stale answer.
Here's the first routine, on the Y button. Read it straight down: send the arm up, wait for it, send it down, wait again, print.
The flywheel's routine ends differently. Canceling a command doesn't stop a motor, so the routine sends the stop itself before it runs out of lines.
A routine is plain Java, so a loop just works. Same four lines, three times round.
Every routine on the page has a timeline behind its code. On this one, look at the arm's lane. It keeps moving while the routine is parked on a wait.
Autonomous changes one thing. Nobody's holding a button, so nobody can let go, and a wait that never comes true would sit there for the whole period.
So every wait gets a limit. Then check which ending you got, because a wait that ran out carries straight on as if the arm had arrived.
Once the flywheel is spinning, every way out stops it first. There are two here, the early one and the normal one.
Now look at the two lanes together. The arm's command is still running underneath while the flywheel spins up and the shot happens, which is the whole reason it was forked.
Before you move on, break it on purpose, twice, and see what each change does. That's the bench mechanisms done. Next the course moves to the drivetrain.
